title: Implement Bubble Sort: compare adjacent elements, swap if wrong order, repeat until sorted; O(n^2) but easy to understand.
keyPoints: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs; the largest value bubbles to the end each pass.
After each pass the largest unsorted element is in its final position, so the inner loop shrinks by one.
A swapped flag allows early exit if a pass completes with no swaps, giving O(n) on already-sorted input.
Time is O(n^2) in worst and average cases; space is O(1); the algorithm is stable.
Bubble sort is a teaching tool, not a production algorithm; it is far too slow for large datasets.
It clearly illustrates the comparison-and-swap mechanic that underpins all comparison sorts.
Java's library sorts (TimSort, dual-pivot quicksort) should always be used in real banking code.

s1_definition.oneliner: Bubble sort repeatedly swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs so the largest value bubbles to the end each pass.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Bubble sort** – a simple comparison-based algorithm that steps through the list, compares adjacent pairs, and swaps them if they are in the wrong order.
- **Bubbling** – after each full pass, the largest remaining element has drifted to its correct position at the end.
- **Early exit** – a `swapped` flag stops the algorithm if a pass completes with no swaps, making it O(n) on sorted input.
- **Stability** – equal elements are never swapped past each other, so their original order is preserved.
- **Quadratic** – O(n^2) in the worst and average cases, making it unsuitable for large data.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India arranging a row of account balances written on cards. The clerk compares the first two cards; if the left one is bigger, she swaps them. Then she compares the second and third, swapping if needed, and keeps moving right. After one full sweep, the largest balance has drifted all the way to the far right, like a bubble rising to the top. She repeats the sweeps until the whole row is sorted.

sections.s6_takeaway:
Bubble sort is the simplest comparison-based sorting algorithm. It steps through the array comparing each pair of adjacent elements and swaps them when they are in the wrong order. After each pass the largest remaining element has bubbled to its final position at the end, so the inner loop shrinks by one.

The one essential optimisation is the `swapped` flag. If a pass completes without any swaps, the array is already sorted and the algorithm exits early, making bubble sort O(n) on sorted input. Without the flag, it always performs the full quadratic work.

Bubble sort is stable because it only swaps adjacent elements when one is strictly greater. It uses O(1) extra space. However, its O(n^2) average and worst-case time makes it unsuitable for any production use at the National Bank of India. It is valuable only as a teaching tool that clearly illustrates the comparison-and-swap mechanic.

The honest senior-level assessment is that bubble sort should never be shipped. For real sorting, use Java's `Arrays.sort` or `Collections.sort`, which are orders of magnitude faster.

Remember one sentence: bubble sort swaps adjacent out-of-order pairs until the largest bubbles to the end each pass, but its quadratic time makes it a teaching tool, not a production algorithm.
